intro: Indian traditions give sharply different answers to what, if anything, the word "I" ultimately refers to. The rows below summarise each tradition's own account.

rows.claim: The Self is pure consciousness, identical with Brahman.
rows.detail: The Self (atman) is the non-dual witness of all experience, never an object. The individual (jiva) is that same consciousness apparently limited by body and mind through ignorance.

rows.claim: The self is an eternal knower, a real mode of Brahman.
rows.detail: Each self (jiva) is eternal, atomic and conscious, and forms part of Brahman's "body". It is wholly dependent on God yet never becomes identical with him.

rows.claim: The self is eternally distinct from God and every other self.
rows.detail: Madhva holds each soul is a conscious, dependent reflection of God with its own inherent nature. Difference between God and souls persists even in liberation.

rows.claim: The Self is one of many pure, inactive witnesses (purusha).
rows.detail: Purusha is consciousness itself, distinct from intellect, ego and mind, which belong to non-conscious prakriti. There are many purushas.

rows.claim: The Self is the seer, apparently coloured by the mind's fluctuations.
rows.detail: Following Sankhya, Yoga holds the seer is pure consciousness. When the fluctuations of the mind-field are stilled, the seer abides in its own nature.

rows.claim: The self is an eternal substance that becomes conscious through a mind.
rows.detail: Consciousness, desire and effort are qualities the self has only when linked with a mind and body. Selves are many and all-pervading.

rows.claim: There is no permanent self; a person is a changing stream of aggregates.
rows.detail: Most schools analyse the person into five aggregates arising dependently. Schools differ: Abhidharma lists momentary elements, Madhyamaka holds even these empty, Yogacara analyses the mind-stream; the Pudgalavadins affirmed an ineffable "person".

rows.claim: The soul is eternal, conscious and naturally omniscient, veiled by karmic matter.
rows.detail: Each jiva is a real, body-sized, conscious agent and knower. Its innate knowledge, perception, bliss and energy are obscured by karma.

rows.claim: The Self is Shiva: free, self-aware consciousness that appears as the individual.
rows.detail: Consciousness is both luminous and self-reflective. The limited self is Shiva freely contracted, and recognising this identity is liberation.

rows.claim: There is no self beyond the living body.
rows.detail: As reported by its critics, Charvaka holds that consciousness emerges from the combination of material elements in the body and ends at death.

note: The disagreement turns on whether consciousness is essential to the self or a quality it acquires, whether there is one self or many, and whether anything enduring underlies experience at all.
